title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Premieres at TIFF: A Movie About a Best Picture Winner That’s a Best Picture Contender?

body:
Yo Adrian, Rocky did it … again!

	Only this time, the famed character is at TIFF in biopic form, thanks to director Peter Farrelly, screenwriter Peter Gamble and a star-making turn from Anthony Ippolito, who portrays actor Sylvester Stallone in the story of his relentless determination to bring “Rocky” to the big screen. This has the DNA of a TIFF Audience winner through and through.


	“I Play Rocky” held its world premiere Saturday night as part of the festival’s Special Presentations program at the Princess of Wales Theatre. It’s one of the very first movies that has played at the festival that has the potential to win TIFF’s highest honor — the People’s Choice Award. Multiple applauses rang throughout the film as the film recreates the highest points of the 1976 MGM flick that became the highest grossing movie of its respective year, went on to be nominated for 10 Oscars, and winning three including best picture. A post-screening Q&A with Farelly, Ipplolito, Stephan James, Jay Duplass and screenwriter Peter Gamble.
	



	

					“I Play Rocky”
									Courtesy of TIFF
	



	There’s a certain symmetry in watching a movie about an unknown who bet everything on himself arrive at the very festival that once turned a modest crowd-pleaser into a best picture winner. Farrelly knows that route. Eight years ago, “Green Book” won the TIFF People’s Choice Award and marched all the way to a best picture statuette. Now the director returns to TIFF with “I Play Rocky,” the story of how a broke, stubborn Sylvester Stallone talked Hollywood into letting him write and star in “Rocky.” 
	

	The film chronicles one of Hollywood’s most improbable success stories: a struggling actor with a script nobody wanted and one nonnegotiable demand — that he play the lead himself. As studios dangle money on the condition that an established star throw the punches, Stallone digs in, turning the standoff that follows into its own kind of prizefight.

	The film’s origin, Farrelly told the Princess of Wales crowd, came down to a script and a self-tape. “I read this script and I thought it was the greatest script I’d ever read,” he said of Peter Gamble’s screenplay, before recounting how the search for his Stallone ended almost before it began. The director said his casting agent called one day claiming to have found the lead — a then-unknown Anthony Ippolito, who had gotten hold of the script and shot three scenes himself in his grandmother’s basement. “I looked at it and the search was over,” Farrelly said. “That’s the guy. We didn’t have to go any further.”

	If the casting feels like fate, that’s because it more or less is. Ippolito, a 27-year-old Long Island native who has been working since childhood, broke out as George Wright in the Netflix drama series “Grand Army” in 2020. He followed with a turn as a young Al Pacino in the Paramount+ limited series “The Offer,” about the making of “The Godfather.” That makes “I Play Rocky” the second time he has played a young Italian American icon at the dawn of a best picture winner — a coincidence too neat to ignore. Make no mistake: a star is born. Ippolito delivers the kind of breakout that turns a working actor into a name overnight, anchoring one of the truest underdog stories the business has ever told. 

	For Ippolito, stepping into the role meant a transformation that stretched across years, not months. “It took a lot of effort, upwards of a year and a half to two years,” the actor told the crowd, thanking Farrelly and the team for the gamble. “I’m just so grateful that they were willing to take a chance on me in this situation.” Then, taking in the room: “This is absolutely surreal.”

	The film carries the same magic and fervor as the 1976 original, and it stands as Peter Farrelly’s finest outing behind the camera — a triumph that plays as both a People’s Choice contender and a genuine Oscar threat. Film Twitter has made its position on Farrelly clear, and the knives will be out again, but that crowd has never been the point. This one is right up the Academy’s alley. The bench is deep, too. AnnaSophia Robb is quietly devastating as Sasha Czack, Stallone’s first wife and earliest believer, while Matt Dillon plays Frank Stallone Sr. Stephan James steps into the trunks as Carl Weathers, the actor who would become Apollo Creed, and Kiki Seto plays Talia Shire opposite Robert Morgan’s Burgess Meredith and Scot Teller’s Burt Young. Jay Duplass rounds out the group as “Rocky” director John G. Avildsen, with P.J. Byrne and Toby Kebbell as producers Irwin Winkler and Robert Chartoff — Byrne proving yet again what a formidable character actor he is, his Winkler nothing short of sublime.
	

	“I Play Rocky” premiered Sept. 12 at the Toronto International Film Festival. Amazon MGM Studios opens the film in limited release Nov. 6, expanding nationwide Nov. 20.

title: Lucy Dacus on Doing a Hollywood Bowl Orchestra Show to End Her ‘Forever Is a Feeling’ Cycle, After Previously Bringing the Boygenius Era to a Close There: ‘Maybe It’s a Place Where I’m Supposed to Cry’
description: “Forever Is a Feeling,” Lucy Dacus promised in the romantic-sounding title of her 2025 solo album. Feelings are transitory things, of course, and so
body:
“Forever Is a Feeling,” Lucy Dacus promised in the romantic-sounding title of her 2025 solo album. Feelings are transitory things, of course, and some of the good ones must come to an end, which is why Dacus is commemorating the end of that era Sunday night with a show at the Hollywood Bowl that will find her accompanied by the Hollywood Bowl Orchestra as well as her touring band. There won’t even be a mid-section where she sends all lthe string and horn players off to take five while she just performs with the band; it’s going to sound lush — and/or, as she promises, “weird” — from start to finish.
	

	Variety spoke with Dacus in the final stages of preparing for this show, discussing what she learned from an earliier incarnation of an orchestra show she did in Chicago; whether she was actually taking requests for this gig; how it feels to return to the site where Boygenius last performed together, three years ago; her side gig presiding over weddings; performing for Mayor Mandani’s inauguration, and much more.


	Recently on social meida you posted a billboard that you or someone took out that said, “Forever is coming to an end,” or something like that.

	“Forever Is Over.”

	“Forever Is Over,” right. Very poetically spoken. But hopefully not in real life.

	Hopefully not in real life, no.

	Is that how you’re thinking of this Hollywood Bowl show, as the grand climax to an era for you?

	Yeah, it’s the last show of “Forever Is a Feeling,” and I really don’t have many plans ongoingly, which kind of freaks me out. But I do feel like I need to mentally understand that it’s over in order to make anything new. So, I think I’ll be really emotional on the day.
	

	I love symphonic shows with the artists I love. I just was at the Bowl and I saw Foo Fighters with an orchestra.

	Cool.

	I’m looking forward to yours more, but it was fun still.

	I won’t tell them.

	We’ll keep that between us. Anyway, you have had a head start now on this, having done an orchestral show in Chicago. Does that make it feel like, you have this aced, it’s gonna go great, we already had a test run on this?

	I learned a lot. I never realized that the musicians don’t look at the material until the day-of, usually. And you get one rehearsal, which is soundcheck, and they’re all just pros and they’re sight reading. That really freaked me out because usually with the band, we’ll practice for a week or more before a tour, and that’s only five people. And I think it’s 50 people on stage for this, and I’m very impressed, and it’s musicianship that feels completely different from what I do. And I have been taking singing lessons trying to prepare, because you have to sing a little bit differently with the orchestra in order to feel like you’re with them and not being completely swallowed by them. So I think that this show will be better than Chicago, just because I was so freaked out in Chicago; now I know how it works.

	I hadn’t heard of anybody going so far as to take singing lessons to learn how to mesh. Do you feel like you figured that out, what the trick is?

	My violinist, Phoenix Rousiamani, did all the arrangements, and she’s brilliant and one of the coolest musical minds I’ve ever known. And the arrangements are weird. They’re not exactly like “Oh, we applied a strings filter to my catalog.” They use really interesting instrument choices and, in some cases, it’s almost like the song is rearranged and has a completely different feel. So I listen to digital bounces of what she did, and I sing to that, and I try to kind of adjust my dynamics to the dynamics that she wrote.

	Some people play the Hollywood Bowl with an orchestra and they’re thinking, “Oh, we’ll just add on some parts that make this feel a little more cinematic,” without reconfiguring anything that they would normally do underneath that. Were you were thinking of song choices that would be most conducive to some sort of approach you wanted to bring?

	Yeah. Phoenix and I listened to everything I’ve ever put out together, and Phoenix was like, “Actually, this song has potential. This song has potential.” And there are more songs that we’re gonna do in L.A. than we did in Chicago. Some of those song choices have to do with songs that I want to play before I stop playing shows for a while. And I have a couple specific songs in mind that I want to sing to people who I know are coming — like, family and friends that I know that they really care about certain songs. So as sort of a gift to them, I was like, “I want to be able to sing this to you in the most dramatic way possible.”
	

	You were on social media a while back when these shows were being announced saying, “Do you guys have anything you wanna hear in this format?” We might have taken that as a token request, assuming you probably already had these arrangements mapped out for a year or something. But you meant it when you were taking suggestions, even though nothing about this suggests something you could rethink on the spur of the moment?

	I feel like I wouldn’t like myself very much if I just emptily asked questions of people like that. But the thing that came around to bite me is that almost every song was requested. So I was like, “Oh, I guess this is for naught.” But I did make some choices because I had all the song names, and then I’d put a tally whenever I saw someone say it. I asked what people wanted, and then a couple days later, I probably spent two hours just scrolling and making tally marks, and the songs that had the most tallies, we definitely prioritized.

	Was there a runaway favorite people asked for that might’ve been unexpected and not necessarily your most popular song?

	Let me look back in my Notes app. I think “Triple Dog Dare” is one that was never a single. It’s really long. I’m really happy, though, that people pull that one out because it’s also one that I like to sing. Let’s see, what else did people say? People say “Kissing Lessons,” so we brought that back, which is fun. Those are the probably two main ones.

	Oftentimes there’ll be a Boygenius song in your set, and in at least some of the normal sets we can look up online, it’ll be “True Blue” or something, which is an obvious choice. But then in Chicago you had “Afraid of Heights,” which was an interesting choice and something that came out kind of late in the Boygenius cycle, so you probably wouldn’t have had a lot of chance to play that anyway. Is that something where you thought, “I want a Boygenius song in here to represent that period, but not one they might expect?”

	Well, Chicago and Toronto were the only cities that I played twice on this album cycle,  in terms of a big production. And people had already heard “True Blue” [in the previous Chicago appearance], and I do like to do one Boygenius song that I wrote. I wrote “True Blue” and I wrote “Afraid of Heights,” so those feel like fair game. I guess anything would be fair game, but it’s nice for me mentally because it feels like my brain switches to a different context, and it’s almost like a little personal intermission to play a Boygenius song and then get back into it. To be clear, though, that [performance of the song in Chicago] was with my band — we had a little couch-section intermission — so the orchestra didn’t do “Afraid of Heights.” But there are some lines in that song that I’m proud of, so I was happy to sing it.
	

	Will it be similar at the Hollywood Bowl, with an orchestra-free couch section in the middle?

	No couch anymore. We did that [in Chicago] because Phoenix very impossibly arranged all of this music in a very short amount of time, compared to how long people usually have. And so now Phoenix has had time to round out the entire set, and so that’s why there’s gonna be more songs.

	Can you say how many songs you ended up arranging for the Bowl show?

	I don’t know how many songs, but I do know that the librettos are 300 pages. Which is really impressive.

	The Hollywood Bowl is not unfamiliar territory for you, with Boygenius having played there, but this is a very different sort of situation. So do you have any feelings about how it feels comfortable ground — “I know this; I made this place my home” — versus still being kind of awed by it in some way?

	I would not say that I am comfortable. I remember playing the Hollywood Bowl with Boygenius on Halloween in 2023, and I had never even been there before. I didn’t understand what we were walking into. And I feel like through the show, I couldn’t process how beautiful it was and the significance of the place. And also, that was our last show, and I was just crying all day. So there’s a part of me that is like, when I arrive, am I gonna be flooded with all of these memories that are gonna be inconvenient for my composure throughout the day? So to finish an album cycle there again does feel like it rhymes with the past. But maybe it’s just a place where I’m supposed to cry. The other time that I went there was for the Joni Mitchell show, where I also cried a lot. So don’t be disappointed if I cannot keep myself together. I’m gonna try my best.

	It’s hard to believe it’s been three years, almost, since the Boygenius Hollywood Bowl show, and the end of Boygenius for the time being.  That was such an intense cycle for you guys. Are you kind of enjoying the relief of doing something else? Or how do you think back on that now since it was so focused for a while?

	I don’t know if I would say it’s a relief in either direction, to do something else or to do Boygenius, or to stop either. I guess I feel the most relief when I’m making things. And so it’s actually like I’m approaching this uncomfortable feeling of being done because I’m like, I want to do this. I want to do shows; I want to make things and keep moving. And slowing down is uncomfortable for me. So I hope that I can at least learn something from it.
	

	Just wrapping up on the Boygenius subject for a second, you’re on Phoebe’s album, and surely you have a strong impression of it. Do you have a thumbnail review of her album, as a friend and a fan?

	I think it’s an instant classic, and I think that she takes her time for a reason, and it’s gonna stand the test of time.

	To rewind to “Forever Is a Feeling,” one of my favorite albums in the last few years, you must have been gratified with the reaction to that. Most fans probably considered it your best album, which, after a while away, has to be what you’re hoping for. In Chicago, again, looking at that setlist, you were doing nine songs from it, maybe even more elsewhere. You must feel as highly about it as your fans do.

	That’s really sweet to say. I feel like it’s a confirmation bias where anyone that shows up to the show loves it, so I don’t really have a finger on the pulse of anything beyond that. But the songs are so special to me on a personal level, and to watch them become special to other people on a personal level throughout this year and year and a half, it’s like one of the magical parts of music — like, they don’t really feel like my life anymore. It feels like just these ideas that all of us can relate to and incorporate into our lives, and that makes me feel connected to everyone that listens to them. And, I don’t know — just in the eternal fight against loneliness, it’s a win.

	Just thinking back on the songs I love on that album, I guess the two that I [most come back to just thinking about in my daily life are “Best Guess” and “Big Deal.” And that must mean I’m a romantic, since those are both kind of swooning in their own way. Although I misunderstood “Big Deal” a little bit when it came out. I saw you mention in a recent interview that it’s a song that was misunderstood in some ways. I was thinking it was after a relationship, looking back on it, but then it was more sort of anticipating or thinking something was gonna happen and then it never did — at least up to that point. Anyway, both very moving songs that must be concert favorites, right?

	Thank you. Yeah, I mean, “Big Deal” is about sort of realizing you have all these feelings, but making all of these efforts to keep it from affecting your life, because you’re not ready for change. But that’s interesting you like those two songs, because it feels like the record starts with “Big Deal,” where you’re not open to feeling what you actually feel, and then “Best Guess” is when you give into it and are like, “You know what? You’re the only future that I’ll accept, and you’re the only thing that makes sense to me in this moment.” And I think that “Big Deal” with the orchestra is my favorite version of it, even more than the recording, and so I’m thankful to Phoenix for that.
	

	And then “Best Guess” means so much now because of all the weddings that I did on stage to that song. And I actually got to see my kindergarten teacher get married to her wife. They’ve been together for, I think, over 30 years, and I was able to go when I was in Richmond, and their first dance was to “Best Guess.” And I was just like, “Who’d have thought when I was 5 years old that I’d be able to write a song that could make my kindergarten teacher happy on this special day?” And so as time goes on, more meaning becomes attached to each of the songs, and it’s part of why I keep doing this at all, is just because that process is really beautiful and humbling.

	Did you sing for your kindergarten teacher for the first dance, or did they just play the recording of the song?

	No, they were like, “You don’t need to sing. Don’t worry.” But I did stand by and give them a thumbs up.

	And how many weddings have you done now, do you know?

	I think it was over 300 people that we married last year.

	Some of those had to have been mass weddings.

	Yeah. They were definitely multiple people at the same time.

	Going back to the Bowl show, you have Cat Power opening. Assuming that was your choice, does that performance has some meaning to you?

	Well, someone on my team was like, “What about Cat Power?” And I was sort of like, “Yeah, right.” And they were like, “Do you want us to ask?” And I was like, “Sure,” just thinking that she wouldn’t say yes, because to me she’s a legend. But she wants to do it, and I have planned my day around making sure that I get to watch her set. Like, there’s a lot going on, but I was like from, you know, from 7 to 8 or 8 to 9 or whatever, I will be watching “The Greatest” by Cat Power. I’ve met her once or twice before, and I just think that her voice and her songwriting and her presence are unmatched. And yeah, that’s another thing that I have against me on the day ,is that I might get so emotional watching that that my show kind of sucks. We’ll see.

	Well, it’s good you mapped it out, that you’re gonna take a time-out there. Since “Planting Tomatoes” was the one new song you’ve had out this year, is that one you’re doing in the L.A. set? It wasn’t in the Chicago orchestral performance.

	I think we’re undecided about that one. I have some ideas for how it could be, but that one is yet to be determined. I can say this: I think that there’s a song that isn’t out yet that will be played at the show.
	

	Your fans are already asking if they’ll get a live record of this. Any chance of that?

	I would say not this show. We looked into it. I mean, there’s boring answers for why it can’t happen. But I would love to document these arrangements someday somehow, which we’ve been talking about, but currently no plans.

	I know there’s something weird about getting the rights for Hollywood Bowl live albums. Anyway, hope you get a shot at it.

	I know. I’m trying my best.

	“Planting Tomatoes,” there’s a lot of your philosophy in that song. Like a lot of your songs, there’s kind of a leavened quality of hope, or it’s cautiously hopeful, or hopefully cautious. There’s a lot of dealing with dark feelings, but with a lot of uplift — that seems to be something you gravitate toward, that’s really embodied in that song.

	Thank you. I feel like I write a lot in my personal life just sitting in the depths of how I feel, and then when I end up writing something that gets to the other side of the depths, it feels more useful somehow to other people. Then again, a lot of the music I love just sits with you in the darkest things, and I’ve been thinking about that recently — if that has its own use. Or, why am I so focused on having something useful to say. But, we all know that there’s just endless strife and struggle and grief, but we have to keep living. So basically, the question of how to carry on and actually enjoy this life and stay connected to what matters to us, that’s kind of an ongoing question that will hopefully have a thousand answers every day. And that song kind of was at least one answer on one day.

	I appreciate that… and I also appreciate the songs that stay at the bottom, too.

	Yeah. Likewise.

	Of course, in recapping your year to date, you sang for the New York mayor’s inauguration. Was that one of the highlights of your year?

	That was, like, the first — I mean, it was literally New Year’s Day, I believe. Yeah, that really set the tone for the year. I don’t think I’ve been so nervous in my entire life, or as cold, gosh, ever. But I think Mandami’s been doing such a great job in New York and I felt so honored to be included, and I hope that the whole world is seeing what’s possible through what he’s doing. And credit to him for choosing “Bread and Roses,” which is a song I love. But it was his idea and a really inspiring song.
	

	You’ve done a lot of playing this year. Do you have a favorite performance up to the Hollywood Bowl?

	Ooh. There’s so many answers I could give. In general, I loved playing the museums and churches at the beginning of this. It wasn’t the full outfit, but we got to exist in some pretty reverent spaces, or I guess I felt reverent within them. Honestly, just recently we played Asbury Park at the Stone Pony Summer Stage, and that was, like, the last show of our proper bus touring with the band, and it was crazy. I was on my ass singing “Night Shift,” and my guitar tech had to come hold the microphone in front of my face. Ratboys and Smidley were running around on stage. My dad was there, and a lot of friends came from Philly. I don’t know, just those moments that I hope the show is good for other people, but I am self-indulgently just enjoying acting up with my friends.

	At the begining of this you sounded a little nervous about not knowing what comes next, but maybe it can be good to know that you don’t have a lot on your agenda after this and that maybe that leaves you wide open for some great ideas.

	Yeah. We’ll see what comes to catch me. I feel like I’m falling, and that hopefully something will just swoop under me and pick me up.

title: ‘SNL U.K.’ Weekend Update Takes Aim at Trump’s New Hair — and Paddy Young Says the Punchline Was ‘Taken From Me by Our Legal Team’
description:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s new hairstyle was heavily mocked in “Saturday Night Live U.K.’s” Weekend Update segment.

	“This week, President Trump
body:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s new hairstyle was heavily mocked in “Saturday Night Live U.K.’s” Weekend Update segment.

	“This week, President Trump stepped off Air Force One sporting a different hair color,” quipped co-anchor Ania Magliano. “He appears to be trialling a new shade of brown. Or, he’s shat his head.”

	“People are questioning, does the carpet still match the drapes?” added Paddy Young. “I wouldn’t know, that’s between the president and the punchline that just a second ago was taken from me by our legal team. Thank you, legal team, it was almost funny.”  It’s unclear whether this moment was a joke, or whether the legal department actually did intervene.
	

	Elsewhere, Prince George’s first day at the prestigious Eton College was imbued with some dark humor. “How will he survive being stuck in a place famous for producing sexual abusers? By leaving it and going to Eton College,” Magliano said to “ooo”s from the audience.


	Recent anti-migrant protests taking place in the U.K. were also under the microscope, including that of far-right activist Danny Tommo. “On Saturday, members of Tommo’s group Patriot Platform yelled obscenities, threw stones, spat and then said goodbye to their families and headed to the protest,” Magliano joked.

	“Who is this Danny Tommo?” responded Young. “Before launching Patriot Platform he is reported to have tried his luck as both a bricklayer and a web designer. However, neither worked out as he had the physique of a web designer and a mind of a brick.”

	The first episode of “SNL U.K.” Season 2 was hosted by Jeff Goldblum.

schema.headline: ‘SNL U.K.’ Weekend Update Takes Aim at Trump’s New Hair — and Paddy Young Says the Punchline Was ‘Taken From Me by Our Legal Team’

title: Paramount Leaving California Would Devastate Los Angeles Economy, Leaked Report Finds
description: A leaked report from the Los Angeles Economic Development Corporation outlines devastating aftershocks that would follow if David Ellison pulled Par
body:
A leaked report from the Los Angeles Economic Development Corporation outlines devastating aftershocks that would follow if David Ellison pulled Paramount Skydance out of California.

	A copy of the report published by Politico reads, “At a minimum, relocating Paramount’s headquarters and other operations out of California would result in losses of 2,750 and 5,550 job-years in California across all industries and losses of between $1.01 billion and $2.03 billion in economic output between October 1, 2026, and September 30, 2031.”
	

	Reps for Paramount had no comment on the matter. 


	In August, news broke of Ellison’s plan to take Paramount Skydance out of the Golden State if California Attorney General Rob Bonta and a coalition of other state AGs did not come to the bargaining table and settle their lawsuit to stop the $111 billion merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Ellison gave the AGs until Oct. 1, or he would start packing. The company is considering states such as Georgia, Texas and Tennessee.

	The report went on to outline some big-picture stats for if and when Paramount Skydance completed the move: “Once Paramount completed the entire relocation of its headquarters and other operations out of California, the state would experience the permanent loss of approximately 28,990 to 57,980 full-time jobs statewide across all industries, and losses of between $10.6 billion and $21.2 billion annually in economic output.”

	On Oct. 1, Paramount Skydance will have to start paying a “ticking fee” to Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders of $7 million a day until the deal closes. The trial between Ellison and the AGs is scheduled to start on March 2, meaning that without a settlement, Paramount is on the hook for about $1.3 billion to WBD shareholders.
	

	In late August, progress toward a settlement seemed promising after Bonta and Ellison scheduled a meeting on Aug. 24. In a last-minute move, Bonta canceled the meeting, accusing the Paramount camp of leaking details of their discussions. Paramount denied the accusations, but Bonta did not relent, saying in a statement he won’t return to settlement talks until they put a “lid on their lying leaks.”

schema.headline: Paramount Leaving California Would Devastate Los Angeles Economy, Leaked Report Finds

title: Jeff Goldblum Performs a Jazz Number to Open ‘SNL U.K.’ Season 2: ‘Hoping You’ll Like Me More Than Nando’s or Marmite’
description: Jeff Goldblum kicked off his hosting duties on “Saturday Night Live U.K.” by employing his musical skills in a jazzy number about spending time in L
body:
Jeff Goldblum kicked off his hosting duties on “Saturday Night Live U.K.” by employing his musical skills in a jazzy number about spending time in London. 

	“Can you believe this is Saturday night, first of all?” Goldblum asked the live audience after making his grand entrance. “And me, I’m hosting this gosh darn ‘SNL U.K.’ triumphant second season first episode! So, for the occasion, may we perform something we’ve just composed special for you tonight?”
	

	The American actor, who has his own jazz band in addition to starring in franchises like “Wicked” and “Jurassic Park,” then took a seat behind the piano and began to sing a tune chock-full of U.K. references. “I’m hoping to be your precise cup of tea and that you’ll like me more than Nando’s or Marmite,” Goldblum sang. “Even if I still bomb, I will keep calm and carry on because I’m hosting from London tonight.”


	Goldblum danced around the stage and even made a reference to his “Wicked” role, singing: “Despite a few wicked flaws, I am the Wizard of Oz!”

	Musical guest CMAT then came out to help Goldblum with the lyrics, holding cue cards that read “Life Finds a Way,” in reference to his famous “Jurassic Park” line. “I don’t recognize it,” Goldblum said — but then the band begin to play the “Jurassic Park” theme and he remembered who he was. “I get it now, I can do it!” 

	“Life finds a way, when you’re live on Saturday,” he concluded with a big finish. “Like Sainsbury’s Local, we’re all feeling vocal. And I’m hosting right here, in London tonight!”

schema.headline: Jeff Goldblum Performs a Jazz Number to Open ‘SNL U.K.’ Season 2: ‘Hoping You’ll Like Me More Than Nando’s or Marmite’

title: ‘SNL U.K.’ Mocks Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s British Return in Cold Open: ‘Don’t Tell Me You’ve Spent All Your Netflix Money Already!’
description: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s recent much-publicized return to England was mocked in the cold open of the first episode of “Saturday Night Live U
body:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s recent much-publicized return to England was mocked in the cold open of the first episode of “Saturday Night Live U.K.” Season 2.

	The cold open began with Larry Dean as King Charles II and Emma Sidi as Queen Camilla relaxing at Balmoral Castle in Scotland (“I do love our weekends away. No responsibilities, just like every other day,” says Camilla.)


	They are then interrupted by the arrival of Harry (Jack Shep) and Meghan (Ayoade Bamgboye). With much of the skit consisting of them being in a close embrace — to the disgust of King Charles — there were countless one-liners making fun of their decision to return to the U.K.
	

	“What do you two want?” asked an infuriated Charles. “Don’t tell me you’ve spent that Netflix money already.”


	“Daddy, it was $16 million,” replied Harry. “How long was it supposed to last?”

	“What a waste you’ve become, you’re lucky your father is not around to see this,” Charles responded, a line which received a large reaction in the room.

	Meghan’s lifestyle brands were also riffed on, with her presenting an ice tray to Camilla. “I made it myself,” she said. “I can give you the recipe. I’m a whizz in the kitchen.”

	“She hires the best chefs,” Harry added.

	George Fouracres, who received acclaim for his acute portrayal of former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, also made his first appearance as Prime Minister Andy Burnham, wearing his trademark black rimmed glasses. 

	“I’m the new PM. And I’m nothing like the last one,” he said. Making fun of Burnham’s raft of policies over the summer and his attempts at being relatable despite being in high office, the skit ended up with him saying: “I will buy everybody a pint, because I want you to like me. I need you to like me.”
	

	The first episode of “SNL U.K.” was hosted by Jeff Goldblum, who performed a jazzy number about spending time in London during his monologue.

schema.headline: ‘SNL U.K.’ Mocks Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s British Return in Cold Open: ‘Don’t Tell Me You’ve Spent All Your Netflix Money Already!’

title: ‘Everybody Wants to F— Me’ Review: Giddily Genre-Crossing Comedy Sees Right Through Taron Egerton’s Nice-Guy Act
description: Just when the victim/villain discourse about sleeper smash “Obsession” was finally beginning to die down, along comes “Everybody Wants to Fuck Me” —
body:
Just when the victim/villain discourse about sleeper smash “Obsession” was finally beginning to die down, along comes “Everybody Wants to Fuck Me” — another story of a young man’s desires getting violently over-satisfied — to start it all up again. Merging romantic comedy, body horror and gender-war satire as casually as its handsome, outwardly affable protagonist gets women into bed (and then, crucially, out of it), this limber first feature from British writer-director Jonathan Schey is alternately silly, nasty fun for much of its running time, carried by a performance of witty good sportsmanship from Taron Egerton, though it’s occasionally hobbled by sexual politics that are slightly less progressive than it seems to think.
	

	Following a hot-ticket premiere at Toronto — where a queue snaking fully around two city blocks proved the value of that deliciously grabby title — “Everybody Wants to Fuck Me” has all the makings of a viral conversation piece once it gets out into the real world, though its genre bait-and-switch move may divide viewers, as the initial promise of a smart, relatable modern-romance study takes a hard-left turn into supernatural territory, complete with inflamed STI imagery to make David Cronenberg proud. (Hey, depending on who you’re talking to, that’s modern romance too.) But that harder-edged novelty should serve Schey’s film well in a market that’s less accommodating of old-school romcoms: As a debut, it’s especially slick and canny, heavily indebted to recent Scandi relationship comedies in its arch tone and playful style, and Schey could follow it down any number of plausible commercial paths.
	

	It’s the poster for Agnès Varda’s feminist touchstone “Cléo from 5 to 7” on his bedroom wall that immediately raises questions about personable, clean-cut Adam (Egerton), and you can practically see them whirring through the mind of Liv (“How to Have Sex” star Mia McKenna-Bruce, in a too-brief cameo) when she wakes up in his bed one sunny Sunday morning. Great film, sure, but is he actually a fan? He might be: He’s urbane and intelligent, works as an associate in a private London gallery dedicated to showcasing female artists, and carries his things around a blue Mubi tote that will get a guffaw of recognition from any industry-adjacent audience. 

	But it could as easily be a performative signal, like the books by Ottessa Moshfegh and Edna O’Brien on his shelf or the adorably scruffy, heterochromic dog named Alana (yes, after Haim) that he walks every day in Victoria Park — accessories that advertise to women his sensitivity, his sophistication, his sharing of their interests. We’ve already seen that Adam is a smooth operator in that regard. In the film’s opening scene, he picks up Liv at a club by intervening when another man is pestering her, pretending to be her boyfriend to fend him off; it’s a nice-guy ploy that secures a one-night stand, though she’s baffled by his standoffishness in the cold light of day. 

	That’s just his routine, however. His WhatApp is a sea of young women similarly seduced and abandoned: The only member of the opposite sex he’ll go out with more than once is his lesbian bestie Emma (Charly Clive), who rolls her eyes at his exploits, but also, as a shacked-up woman with a baby on the way, vicariously lives through them a little. Significantly less forgiving, however, is Sofia (a scintillating Jessica Henwick), the cynical academic type he tries to pick up at the theater, and who calls him out on pretty much all his shit from the get-go, spitting out the script’s most immediately quotable line: “Men don’t actually like women — they just want women to like them.” 

	Against all odds, she invites Adam back to her place, where her take-control attitude both confuses and excites him, and the night gets blurrier from there. The next morning, she‘s the one who’s ghosted him, and from then on, nothing quite feels right, even though he’s suddenly sending out pheromones that appear to make him absolutely irresistible to women. Even by his promiscuous standards, his body count soars; simple eye contact, it seems, is enough to seal the deal. So why isn’t he having more fun? Why does it feel like he isn’t actually doing the work here? And what’s that purply welted rash forming down in his crotch? Schey deftly builds this uncanny turn of events by degrees, in such a way that we’re initially unsure if Adam is simply delusional, but also isn’t shy of exploring its most extreme possibilities for darkly farcical purposes. Suffice it to say that incest isn’t off the table.
	

	Egerton’s initially cocksure, steadily more frantic performance does much to sell this absurd pivot, lending proceedings a recognizable human factor throughout: We all know men a bit like Adam, who aren’t the worst but are also pretty far from the best, who may not be overtly toxic themselves, but don’t recognize the toxicity inherent in their advantaged social status. “Everybody Wants to Fuck Me” allows us to feel a little sorry for him, while also relishing the spectacle of him being put through the wringer a bit — especially as the film’s grosser horror instincts take over. 

	It’s just a bit of a shame that Schey’s script winds up advocating for a pretty staid alternative to his behavior in Emma’s thoroughly domesticated monogamy and imminent parenthood: There are safe, fun, equitable ways to, well, be a horny little devil, and this lively, zesty, thoroughly enjoyable comedy could spend a little more time exploring the options and playing the field.

schema.headline: ‘Everybody Wants to F— Me’ Review: Giddily Genre-Crossing Comedy Sees Right Through Taron Egerton’s Nice-Guy Act

title: ‘Letters From the Silenced Country’ Wins Golden Globes Impact Prize for Documentary Presented During Venice Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Belarusian director Andrei Kutsila’s “Letters from the Silenced Country,” a portrayal of contemporary Belarus seen through the lives of five individ
body:
Belarusian director Andrei Kutsila’s “Letters from the Silenced Country,” a portrayal of contemporary Belarus seen through the lives of five individuals whose existence has been upended by state violence and political repression, is the winner of The Golden Globes Impact Prize for Documentary awarded in partnership with Artemis Rising Foundation at the Venice Film Festival.

	The juried prize, which honors a documentary filmmaker with a feature in the 2026 Venice official selection that calls attention to a key social issue with journalistic and creative prowess, is presented at the fest as a collateral impact award.
	

	Built around personal letters written from prison, exile, and underground life, “Letters from the Silenced Country” – which premiered at Venice out-of-competition – combines observational documentary, archival footage, and animation based on drawings created in confinement. “Rather than a broad political overview, the film focuses on individual stories, of protest, imprisonment, escape, and everyday resistance, told through the people living them,” according to a provided synopsis.


	The Golden Globes Impact Prize for Documentary Award’s jury at Venice comprised Filipino-American star Liza Soberano; Golden Globes president Helen Hoehne; Oscar-winning producer and founder of Artemis Rising Foundation Regina K. Scully; Oscar-winning producer and co-founder of Impact Partners Geralyn White Dreyfous; and founder and CEO of Think-Film Impact Production, Danielle Turkov Wilson.

	“Letters from the Silenced Country puts a human face on a crisis too often reduced to headlines and numbers, illustrating the impossible choices people make to hold on to their humanity,” the jury collectively said in a statement. 
	

	“Though it is rooted in Belarus, its story reaches far beyond one country’s borders, it speaks to anyone who has ever loved someone from a distance, or fought to stay connected to who they are under pressure to disappear,” they added. “The way the director blends letters, drawings, and memory into the storytelling captures not only grief, but love, hope, and tenderness – the full range of what it means to remain human. It’s a powerful example of how a documentary can show how the most personal stories can also be the most universal.”

	The prize carries $10,000 in cash from Artemis Rising Foundation.

	Earlier this year, husband-and-wife filmmaking duo Joshua and Rebecca Tickell were jointly awarded the Golden Globes Prize for Documentary awarded in partnership with Artemis Rising Foundation at Cannes.



	

									Courtesy Think-Film
	



	From left to right: Golden Globes President Helen Hoehne, actress Liza Soberano, Venice Film Festival artistic director Alberto Barbera, Think-Film founder and CEO Danielle Turkov Wilson.

schema.headline: ‘Letters From the Silenced Country’ Wins Golden Globes Impact Prize for Documentary Presented During Venice Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Mia Wasikowska Fills Out the Screen As ‘Agata the Writer’ in Kuba Dorabialski’s Venice Drama: ‘It’s Our Responsibility to Understand Each Other’
description: Mia Wasikowska fills out the screen in Kuba Dorabialski’s “Agata the Writer.” Metaphorically and figuratively, as one especially arresting sequence
body:
Mia Wasikowska fills out the screen in Kuba Dorabialski’s “Agata the Writer.” Metaphorically and figuratively, as one especially arresting sequence shows her in close-up looking directly at the audience and recounting the rest of the story.  

	“I was so curious about it,” she says.  

	“Luckily, when I’m doing something, I don’t think too much about how it’s going to be perceived. Kuba sent me some references, which I thought were really interesting, and it felt organic. But then, when I was watching the scene, I thought: ‘Ok. That’s enough of my face’!”
	

	Known for blockbusters like “Alice in Wonderland” and high-profiles dramas “Stoker” or “Jane Eyre,” Wasikowska has been pursuing arthouse fare in recent years. 

	“I was really excited about making a film that didn’t follow a typical narrative structure. I feel like we have tunnel vision about how to tell a story and make a film,” notes Wasikowska. She also executive produced the film. 

	“This brings back the sense of exploration. I’m very proud it was made in a market that’s increasingly myopic about how it’s done.”

	A Whitefalk Films and Produktion Productions production – sold by French sales company MMM Film Sales – sees Wasikowska as Agata, a Polish-Australian writer who arrives in Sarajevo to write about the war. She wants to speak to the survivors, but they question her motives. Not to mention, weird artworks start to mysteriously disappear from the house where she’s staying.

	Dorabialski wanted to combine cinema and literature in the film.
	

	“How do you make these two very different but also very interconnected forms of expression work? Reading is a solitary practice, and we experience cinema collectively,” he states. 

	He was been back and forth about the title pretty much until the premiere in Venice. 

	“And then, suddenly, I felt affection for it. I have a lot of affection also for writers too. The essence of everything I’m interested in is this very particular magic of literature. But where it falls short is silence and stillness. Even a novel that explores silence has to fill that void with language. Cinema has the audience in chains, dictating how long stillness lasts,” he says.

	“I think these two forms complement each other beautifully.”

	Dorabialski comes from the world of video art, where “formal experimentation is not only kind of acceptable – it’s necessary.” 

	“Cinema felt really exciting to me precisely because it has rules. There’s a definite beginning and end time; there’s a dark room and a screen. We’re just brains in a void. I was excited by some of that formal restriction.”

	Wasikowska and Dorabialski both have Polish roots, but in the film, Agata heads to Sarajevo instead.

	“I was interested in the idea of Slavic identity outside Eastern Europe and what it means to be part of this linguistic ethnic group,” he explains. 

	“Much of my work has examined historical similarities throughout Eastern Europe, politically and linguistically. Bosnia and Poland are about as far apart as two Slavic cultures could be, but the concept of Eastern Europe is formed from outside that territory. It’s always the West and the Anglophone world looking at this region and othering this group. I guess I’m playing the insider-outsider game here.”

	He knew that Wasikowska would be the right Agata. 

	“Partly it’s because she has this Polish-Australian connection, but primarily because of the way she chooses and approaches her roles. I knew she could handle the challenge of playing someone who’s very pensive, restrained, quiet and detached.”

	He adds: “Even in the final act of the film, where there’s nothing but Mia’s face, we’re still listening to the story and engaging with its content. Every time I watch it, I notice all the small decisions she made that give depth to her expressions.” 
	

	Wasikowska hasn’t really explored her roots before. Edward Zwick’s “Defiance,” about a Jewish underground resistance movement, came the closest. 

	“I haven’t had the opportunity to do that too much. But just from growing up, it’s very familiar to me,” she says. 

	“My mum and grandma were immigrants, and I observed their experience of trying to find belonging while being nostalgic about Poland. I’ve also traveled back to Poland many times. I connected with that in the script, and with Kuba. I understood the search for belonging and the feeling of being in between cultures even when somewhere feels familiar.”

	That’s Agata’s struggle as well, as she’s desperately trying to figure out how to write about a conflict she hasn’t experienced. And whether it even makes sense. 

	“To me, what’s meaningful is the intention of trying to understand other people and things we haven’t lived through. That’s what it means to be human. It’s our responsibility to try to understand each other,” says Wasikowska. 

	And, according to Dorabialski, artists have a responsibility to respond to the world in which they live. 

	“It’s not like you go to church and all your sins are forgiven just because you’ve made an artwork about Gaza. But shouldn’t we expect art to create change? I’m not convinced that it does, especially in any kind of lasting, meaningful way. But artists have to do it anyway.”

schema.headline: Mia Wasikowska Fills Out the Screen As ‘Agata the Writer’ in Kuba Dorabialski’s Venice Drama: ‘It’s Our Responsibility to Understand Each Other’

title: Camera-Shy Chrissie Hynde on Finally Allowing a Definitive Doc to Be Made About ‘The Pretenders,’ Bowing in Toronto: ‘I Just Wanted to Be in a Band. I’ve Never Graduated Beyond That Initial Interest in It’
description: At this late date, what the Pretenders accomplished is no mystery achievement. But it’s also a story that has never been extensively chronicled on
body:
At this late date, what the Pretenders accomplished is no mystery achievement. But it’s also a story that has never been extensively chronicled on film until “The Pretenders,” a Joss Crowley-directed doc that premieres Sunday at the Toronto International Film Festival. The band released what might rightly be considered the best rock ‘n’ roll debut album of all time in Janauary 1980, and Crowley’s film covers the lead-up to that — Chrissie Hynde looking and acting like a biker chick in late ’70s Akron before moving to and finding her real gang in the U.K. — and the tumultuous few years that followed, with further masterpieces arriving alongside band dismisals and deaths. Although the focus is on the original lineup and the first five years, it brings us into the present day of Hynde, still one of the greatest to ever pick up a guitar.

	As delightfully plain-spoken as Hynde is when you get her to sit down and talk, she can be difficult to get into that chair, as a naturally camera-shy personality, so Crowley’s film is particularly useful in further immortalizing a subject who never wanted to be anything more than an ordinary musician, whether “rock goddess” was quickly and eternally thrust upon her or not.

	Variety spoke with Crowley and the charmingly tart-as-ever Hynde in advance of the Toronto premiere.

	Most of the time with modern music documentaries, it’s the artist or their company instigating the doc, and usually co-producing it. But it sounds like that’s not necessarily what happened this time because, Joss, you’ve talked about the difficulty in talking Chrissie into it.

	Joss Crowley: I’ve been trying to work with Chrissie and tell the Pretenders’ story for over 10 years, and kept knocking at the door; didn’t get an answer. It was just a question of right time, right place, and Chrissie came round to the idea of meeting me. We sat down and talked about some of the docs I’ve made, and about other things, trying to find some mutual interests. I wasn’t really sure when I left that meeting how it had gone, but within about a week, we sat down and recorded our first interview, at the end of 2023.

	Chrissie, you needed less than a week to think about it and get underway after that first meeting?

	Chrissie Hynde: Well, we had to have a go and see how it would go, and I think I must have laid down some sort of ground rules, so I was willing to go into it — that it would be (visually focused on) archive footage, and really talk about the band and not focus too much on me, and it wouldn’t be about “women in rock” or any of that kind of thing. It would just be a story of the band. I was kind of keen to have it done because, as we all know, there’s documentaries on everything and everyone now. And in fact, someone else had already made a documentary on the Pretenders, which had nothing to do with me or my entire organization. I was starting to get calls from some of my old friends saying, “Oh, I’m gonna do your documentary on Tuesday.” And I’d be like, “We’re not doing a documentary!” This other team had gone in to people I know and made it sound like it was an official documentary. So I thought, “Well, if that’s happened once, that’s gonna happen again.” Either you want to do it and you want your story out, or you don’t, which I didn’t particularly, but if it’s going to be out, I’d rather know that it’s true.



	

					Chrissie Hynde in ‘The Pretenders’
									Courtesy TIFF
	



	At the very end of the film, you’re heard talking a little bit about why you did it and you mention that you especially wanted to do it for James Honeyman-Scott [who suddenly died at the height of the band’s success in 1981], in some way.

	Hynde: For me, a rock band is all about electric guitar, and I think he was one of the great guitar heroes. Over the years when I see lists of the greatest 100 rock guitar players, I never see Jimmy’s name. That’s all he was interested in, music and playing the guitar, and I thought he didn’t get his due and that would be important for him. He’s not here, so I thought I could do it for him.

	It feels like the way the documentary turned out was kind a nice compromise in the end, since you didn’t want to be on-camera at all, but you were talked into being seen for the very last interview, so there’s a little bit but not a lot. You acquiesced a little bit.

	Hynde: Yeah. I haven’t seen it, and I probably won’t. Someone said, “Oh, don’t say that! That sounds negative.” But I think a lot of people don’t like watching themself or listening to themself talk, and I don’t have to watch it, and there you go. It’s not negative. I mean, I’ve already lived through it, so I don’t think I wanna go through it all again.


	I think so many people feel this way, and most people that I’ve ever had a conversation about it with do: they don’t like the sound of their speaking voice. I mean, I’ve had to get used to my singing voice because, you know, that’s kind of my shtick. But my speaking voice, when I hear it back, I’m always pretty horrified. And everyone I talk to feels the same way… People expect if you do it for a living, that you must like it, but that’s not necessarily true.


	One of your quotes in here is, “I like being in a band, I just don’t like being observed. It’s a real problem.” A lot of people will relate to that, wanting to have a voice — figuratively — while not liking the attention that comes with it.
	

	Hynde: I think so, because I think I represent just ordinary people, and that’s how I feel and that’s how I go through my life. You know, I get the public transport. I don’t live in a gated community. I’m just exactly the same way I always was, and I don’t want that taken away from me. I like hanging out. I’d rather sit on a doorstep and eat a slice of pizza than go to a fancy restaurant. I’ve always been like that, but I think most people are.


	It has become more common in documentaries to have the subjects entirely off-screen. I was recently watching Paul McCartney’s Wings documentary, and his interviews in it are all audio-only, which is great most of the time. But at the same time you’re kind of like, “Well, just show him to me for 10 seconds.”

	Hynde: Are you talking about “Man on the Run”? I loved that. In fact, I watched it sitting next to Paul when it was screening. He was singing along! I guess he’s so used to seeing himself. It was very moving for me to see Linda in the early days, even before I met her, and how cool and how beautiful she was… We’ve seen so many documentaries, it’s a matter of kind of getting away from the format. But, certainly, archive footage — we were lucky to have any for ours, because this was way before people had camera phones or were thinking much about taking photos.
	

	Crowley: There was a big archive breakthrough when we found this cameraman, Andy Watt, who’s from Hereford, like the band really, and he joined the original band on tour about three months before Pete left and Jimmy died. [Bassist Pete Farndon was dismissed in 1982 and died the following year; Honeyman-Scott died two days after Farndon’s firing.] He was able to document two weeks on the road in North America with the band, and that footage has never been seen. We found all 20 tapes of it, and they were in very poor condition and pretty much unusable, but fortunately we found a retired engineer who was able to bring them back to life. Another thing that really helped the device was doing the interviews with Stan, the old tour manager, who read his diaries aloud, and we could suddenly see Jimmy and Pete in and around the band in the period where we focused the story, which is those five years between the end of the ’70s and the early ’80s.

	You start the movie with Stan Tippins, now an elder gent, reading these diaries for the camera. It seems like his participation was really, no pun intended, a tipping point.

	Hynde: I’d love to see that stuff, with the Stan diaries. All the time that we were with Stan, he often mentioned, “Now I’m gonna go write my diary,” but no one ever saw them. Joss and I had dinner with Stan and Lynne Honeyman-Scott, Jimmy’s sister, and (original drummer) Martin Chambers, and it never even occurred to me that Stan would be willing to be actually filmed, reading his diaries. I’m dying to see all that part, so maybe I will have to watch it at some point. Stan was so important in the early band. He was our scout leader or something. We were new at this, and he had been a singer in Mott the Hoople [prior to Ian Hunter]. We loved him, because was like having a farmer in a band. He would say things like, “I don’t know why you would wanna take drugs when you could have a nice, juicy pear.” I suppose you could say we were laughing behind his back, but he was the wise man of the operation.

	When it came to your interviews, Chrissie, there ae some topics that are tricky or touchy, inevitably. It’s clear on camera when you are willing to get into something and when you aren’t. Joss asks you about Ray Davies, and you say, “I’d rather not get into it. There’s a lawsuit waiting to happen.” But it’s cool that we at least see you address not wanting to discuss something, whereas a lot of docs would just leave that out. And then, of course, you do get into a lot of tough stuff with the early ’80s with everything that happened with the band. Was it cathartic in any way to talk about the hard times of the band, or is it always just difficult?

	Hynde: First of all, talking about, for example, Ray Davies — I mean, anything with him or with anyone in my family — I don’t think it’s right to talk about other people because it’s an invasion of their privacy. I’ve never done that, and I don’t think that’s a very dignified thing to do. If people ask me, “Oh, are your kids musical?” I say, “Well, if you ever meet them, you ask them. I don’t wanna talk about it.” Not because I don’t love them, but because this is kind of an invasion of their privacy. And I’ve never talked to any journalist and given a list of things that they’re not allowed to ask. Because if I don’t wanna talk about it, then I can say, “Let’s not talk about it.” But not for any other reason than that. Because certainly as a Kinks fan, I mean, who doesn’t wanna talk about Ray Davies? He’s fucking amazing. But I just don’t do that.
	

	I can’t remember what Joss asked me about the grisly stuff in the ’80s, because I haven’t revisited that. But the other thing is, when you have a story that’s in public or when you become famous or whatever, your story isn’t that much more interesting than just an ordinary person’s. I mean, nobody hasn’t had bereavements and fuck-ups and disappointments and victories, and all these things that happen in a person’s life. I think there’s too much emphasis on the extraordinary life of celebrities.

	You’ve been clear from the beginning of your career up till now that you never wanted to be a poster girl or an emblem or spokesperson for anything.

	Hynde: Being in a rock band… I mean, who didn’t wanna be in a rock band? Did you wanna be in a rock band?

	Of course.

	Hynde: Are you now?

	No, sadly.

	Hynde: But you wanted to be. So, I’ve offered some music, and that’s all I’m offering. Everyone that I grew up with wanted to be in a rock band. That was my generation. We were all very ordinary kids. People didn’t get into bands to become celebrities. They just wanted to be in a band. I’ve never graduated beyond that initial interest in it.
	

	Surely you’ve grown in a thousand ways since the band’s early days, but the film kind of presents you as somebody who sort of had either a certain idealism or just a basic attitude about certain things and stuck to it.

	Hynde: I also had some great people that I’ve met in my life who were inspirational. Lemmy never changed. Lemmy was always the same. and that’s kind of been my motto. That’s why I don’t do fashion magazines. Well, there’s many reasons I don’t! But I always think, “Well, if you wouldn’t ask Lemmy to do it, don’t ask me.” Because he’s kind of, I suppose you could say, my style icon, if there is such a thing in the case of someone who was in Motörhead.

	Neil Young’s another. He’s never changed. You might not have ever met him, but anyone who’s listened to his music, you have met him. He’s exactly what you think he’s going to be. Bob Dylan, I mean, is obviously more of an enigma, because he’s a little bit more of a trickster and a comedian. But he offered the world all that music and I’m not sure that he got into it to be the spokesman of his generation, which was the mantle that he had to carry. And in the case of Willie Nelson, Neil Young, Bob… First name basis, did you get that? [Laughs.] Paul McCartney’s the best example because he was in the fucking Beatles, and yet he’s still doing exactly what he was doing. If his band hadn’t made it that big, I reckon if he was still in Liverpool and he got married and had some kids, he’d probably still be playing in a band in a local bar somewhere, because that’s what he likes.

	Joss, is there any way to put in a nutshell what you wanted to capture about Chrissie in this film? And did it change at all as you spent so many hours with her?
	

	Crowley: To answer the first question, it’s the story of the Pretenders, which I know is obviously very much about Chrissie, but also about the rest of the band. But with Chrissie, because I spent so many hours with her, I just wanted to make sure her personality came across in the film. Because I think that’s what documentary does perhaps better than any other medium, is that it brings personality to the screen. And so if it felt awkward at times, that’s OK. When it was successful, great. When the band was successful, great. And everything in between, and when it was emotional and sad, it had to be there. We were talking about voices earlier on, and I’ve had to get used to hearing my voice a bit because it was important to hear questions that I put to Chrissie that she didn’t want to answer, or at least didn’t want to answer initially and then came round to answering later on. Because that, I think, tells you as much about Chrissie as a perfectly articulated answer. So that was something I guess I warmed up to, the idea of keeping my questions in, which I haven’t done in previous documentaries. That was a good way to unlocking a bit more about who Chrissie is.

	The other question: in terms of hours, we would meet monthly, for a few hours…

	Hynde: Seems like most of my life. No, Joss did prompt me, but mainly I just imagined a certain time, an event that happened, and I would just talk about it for an hour, and then have a few cups of tea and leave. And then he’d have to figure it out. Definitely the early sessions were much more like that, and as it evolved, it became a bit more interview-based, I suppose, and it had a different rhythm to it.

	I didn’t want to ask my mates to sit down in front of a camera, because I find it uncomfortable, so I thought, “Well, why would I expect them to do it?” So I made a real point of just having talk-over [i.e., audio-only interviews]. But then you have to think about, if you’re on stage, what are you prepared to do? But then you also have to think about the audience: What do they want? And I’ve been in the audience as much as I’ve been on stage, if not more. I know the audience wants a certain thing. And [for a documentary] I know the audience wants to see people sitting down talking to camera. I know I want to see that.

	Crowley: There were two things that Chrissie said to me early on in the process. She said, “Make it good, and make it different.” And I think we’ve achieved that. But you can’t make something different for the sake of it being different. It has to work for the story that the film tells. And Chrissie doesn’t like cameras. Chrissie doesn’t like having her photograph taken. It was really hard to find archive as well because lots of times cameramen or camera crews weren’t allowed access to the band. It was hard on a lot of levels. So the fact that I managed to to convince Chrissie to go on camera for the final interview, it just sort of works. I think it’s an achievement of the film and also a reflection of how much she doesn’t want to be on camera all the time.

	You probably did get much more intimate stuff by allowing her to just speak into a microphone. And we get to luxuriate in the sound of her voice as she’s digging deep on some of that stuff…

	Hynde: Oh, God, when you said “luxuriate in the sound of her voice,” I’m cringing.

	You often say you don’t like to be a symbol of anything, but is anything you represent to the public that you kind of allow for yourself as being OK?

	Hynde: Well, of course I like being a sex symbol, but…

	Glad you brought that up, because that was something that struck me watching the movie — that to some people you were and are a sex symbol, and at the same time, there is Shirley Manson talking about how what you got out of it was loving seeing you be androgynous, so…
	

	Hynde: I was being facetious! [About being a sex symbol.] I’m just, you know… I’m a man of the people.

	One thing that hasn’t changed that you represent: being against rock turning completely consumerist. Every time I see a music star doing a product commercial, I think of your song “How Much Did You Get for Your Soul?”

	Hynde: Yeah. They’re all at it, aren’t they? Well, you know, fuck ’em.

	Joss, do you have a favorite moment in the movie?
	

	Crowley: Favorite part of the production of making the film, I guess, was when Stan opened his diaries for the first time, and he found the first time he met Chrissie in rehearsals, because it was such a breakthrough for me. I think he summed up quite a lot about, about Chrissie and the band in a few words. Do you know the bit I’m talking about? I can’t remember exactly what he says, but it’s something like, “She has quite a lot of fun, but underneath she might be a bit nervous.”

	Hynde: Oh, God, I hate to think what’s in those diaries. Fuck me. But we love Stan, so there you go.

	Chrissie, we can’t ask you if you have a favorite moment in the movie…

	Hynde: I saw my manager, Ian Grenfell, yesterday and I said, “Hey, is this gonna come across really negative if I say I haven’t watched it?” And he goes, “Don’t worry about it, because that horse has bolted. People already know [to expect] you haven’t watched it. And a lot of people do not watch their documentaries.” So I was relieved that I don’t have to tough it out… I’ve been very inspired in the last couple of days, seeing Noel and Liam (Gallagher, from Oasis) out there. They’ve got a documentary out and they’re on the front line going for it. But I just don’t have that kind of drive.

	I’m sure you’ll be in Toronto, Joss. Are you going, Chrissie, or will you be avoiding the premiere?

	Hynde: Yeah, I am going. And then Martin’s going. It’s gonna be me and Martin there on the red carpet, so that should be… Well, it won’t be a beauty contest.

schema.headline: Camera-Shy Chrissie Hynde on Finally Allowing a Definitive Doc to Be Made About ‘The Pretenders,’ Bowing in Toronto: ‘I Just Wanted to Be in a Band. I’ve Never Graduated Beyond That Initial Interest in It’

            Lady Gaga's clearly a protective mom ... holding her baby tightly in the first photos taken of the pair together.
      
    
            The singer-songwriter was spotted recently holding her swaddled child close to her chest while walking with her fiancé, Michael Polansky, and a friend.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Gaga kept her head down ... walking quickly with her crew in Northern California -- where Page Six reports she's been laying low in recent weeks to enjoy some private family time.
      

            As we reported ... Gaga and Polansky welcomed a new baby together, though we don't yet know the kid's name, gender or exact date of birth.
      
    
            LG dropped a massive hint that her duo would soon become a trio on "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert" ... when she said her next starring role would be "motherhood."
      
    
            Gaga and Polansky got engaged back in 2024 ... though the two still apparently haven't tied the knot. She said in March they plan to get married "soon."
      
    
            We'll have to wait and see if the baby's birth gets things moving on that front!

                                                                      |

                                  September 12, 2026
                                4:23 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Comedian Charleston White has been arrested for battery in Florida ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            The 49-year-old jokester -- who boasts more than 250,000 subscribers on his YouTube channel -- was arrested by the Hollywood Police Department on Saturday ... according to jail records TMZ obtained.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            White was then booked into Broward County jail on a Touch Or Strike/Battery charge, which is a misdemeanor ... arrest records show.
      

            He will remain on bail until a judge can review his case ... and decide whether or not to set a bond.
      
    
            White is scheduled to have his next show in nearby Naples at the Off the Hook Comedy Club Wednesday night at 7 PM ... we'll see if we find out more about what went down by then.
      
    
            White did not immediately respond to our request for comment.
